• Other names: dwarf rotala, round-leaf toothcup, pink sprite
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0–8.0
  • Optimal GH: 2–12
  • Optimal temperature: 20–28 °C
  • Substrate: needed
  • Growth form: stem
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement: mid-ground or background
  • Height: 5–30+ cm
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: head cuttings or runners

• Type: stem plant
  • Origin: Asia
  • Height: 20–30+ cm after two months in the tank
  • Light demand: medium
  • CO2 demand: medium

Fertiliser is not mandatory, but fertilisers containing micronutrients such as iron are essential for healthy growth. Chelated iron and potassium help it develop vibrant red leaves and prevent stunting. Liquid fertiliser at the planting stage kicks off healthy growth.

Planting: remove from the pot, disinfect and rinse thoroughly, then plant individual stems in holes in the substrate, 3–4 cm apart to avoid overcrowding. Suited to Nature-style and Dutch aquascapes, in the background and mid-ground.

Propagation: cut the top of the stem with sharp scissors; cuttings should be at least 10 cm long. Make a hole of about 3–4 cm in the substrate, insert the stem and cover.

Care: minimal care. It tolerates ammonia, so it easily survives cycling. It can effectively remove nitrogen and phosphorus from water. Remove dead parts and leaves with tweezers to avoid polluting the water, and gently stir dense stems to bring debris to the surface and sieve it out.

Trimming: regular trimming makes it dense. Trim first about 10 cm below the final desired height. As the tops grow, cut those that grow faster than the rest so that shoots branch and the canopy becomes denser. Trimmed parts can be discarded or replanted.

Problems: Chlorosis and necrosis at leaf margins: pale, yellow or yellow-white leaves caused by iron or nitrogen deficiency, or pH below 5.0 or too alkaline; dose chelated iron and keep pH optimal. Stunted growth: too low nitrate, too few trace elements, or no or inadequate CO2; correct these and increase light. Loss of lower leaves: a sign of insufficient light, or planting too densely so the lower part is shaded.
Prune it frequently to maintain healthy growth. An ideal starter plant that looks best when planted in large groups.

Temperature: it tolerates a wide range but thrives best in tropical tanks at 20–28 °C, and can withstand relatively cool temperatures. A submersed population in Wenzhou, Zhejiang, China survives winter at temperatures as low as 4 °C.

pH can range from 6 to 8; test water parameters regularly. Keep hardness at 4–15 °dGH.

Nutrients: keep nitrate below 5 ppm and phosphate above 1 ppm to enhance the reddish colour.

Lighting: often grown in medium light, but needs relatively high light for optimal growth and colour. It appreciates 35–50 PAR from full-spectrum (5000–7000 K) bulbs. Under sufficient bright light the green leaves turn reddish-pink; in low light the plant grows thin and yellow-green.

Substrate: it survives in almost any substrate and can even float. Small-granulated soil gives the best results, with better plant height, tiller number and biomass than sand or gravel. It thrives in nutrient-rich substrates such as ADA Amazonia soil, Caribsea Eco-Complete and Seachem Flourite Black Sand. With sand or gravel, use root tabs from time to time.

CO2: it does well without CO2 injection after an adjustment period, but additional CO2 gives better density, faster growth and better colour.

Rotala rotundifolia is a perennial aquatic plant native to South East Asia, family Lythraceae (order Myrtales). The name comes from Latin words meaning 'the plant with rounded leaves'. The genus Rotala consists of fast-growing stem plants, widely used in aquascaping for their colour, which varies from green to red or reddish-pink depending on the species.

It has distinct emersed (terrestrial) and submersed forms. In the emersed form the leaves are round and thicker, whereas in the submersed form they are narrow, thin and lanceolate. It can grow up to 30 cm.

It is an aquatic, amphibious, tropical and sub-tropical plant with considerable phenotypic plasticity, growing as an obligate aquatic in shallow water, and also in semi-aquatic or terrestrial habitats. It is found mainly in South-east Asia, including Japan, China, Taiwan, Laos, Vietnam, Thailand and India, where it grows as a weed in rice paddies, low-lying fields, marshes and swamps.

It has also been introduced to the United States, where it was declared invasive in some areas. It was listed as a Category One invasive species by the Florida Exotic Pest Plant Council in 2007; it is no longer listed as a potential threat by other US states, but is a recognised weedy invasive species in Australia.

The stems are soft, branch to form low creeping clumps, and are pink. Leaves are often 2.5 cm or less and grow in clusters of 2 or 3 around the stem. The plant forms aerial roots, and its stems act like stolons, bending towards the ground. Spikes of small pink flowers form only on aerial or emergent tips. It spreads vigorously by stem fragments that root at lower nodes and also produces viable seeds that germinate under favourable conditions.

Related species: Rotala indica (sometimes called Rotala 'Bonsai') was previously confused with R. rotundifolia; it is smaller, used in nano tanks, with rounder, greener leaves, and needs medium light and additional CO2. Rotala macandra (giant rotala, King of the Reds) has broader oval leaves with wavy margins, grows to 40–50 cm and is demanding: acidic water, lots of iron, water movement, CO2 and strong light. Rotala wallichii has a single unbranched stem up to 40–50 cm, with needle-like whorled leaves 10–12 mm long and 1.25 mm wide.

Benefits: suited to jungle aquascapes; leaves provide a large surface for biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets; provides shelter for shy fish and shrimp; removes excess nutrients and nitrates; oxygenates the water; its roots help break up anaerobic pockets (hydrogen sulfide, H2S, smells like rotten eggs and can be dangerous to fish and shrimp); it can accumulate heavy metals and may be used in wastewater treatment; and it inhibits algae by outcompeting them for nutrients. Algae-eating species such as Amano shrimp, nerite snails and otocinclus can be added to help.

Tankmates: compatible with most freshwater fish and invertebrates because it is hardy and non-toxic: guppies, mollies, swordtails, angelfish, loaches (clown loach, coolie loach), discus, platies, tetras, zebra danio, otocinclus; all Neocaridina and Caridina shrimp, Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp; snails such as ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor and mystery snails (beware snails that damage plants). Avoid aggressive fish that tear up plants, such as oscars, Frontosa, Texas cichlids, red devils and Jack Dempsey. Do not keep it with crayfish or crabs, which uproot plants. Compatible plants: Anubias nana, Anacharis, Java fern and water wisteria.

Buying: inexpensive and widely available. Choose plants without cuts, holes or tears in the leaves, with bright green or reddish leaves and healthy stems and roots.

Quarantine: the plant may carry parasites, pests such as snails, or predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.), and may have been treated with pesticides that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

The Asiatic Rotala sp. 'Green' is very similar to Rotala rotundifolia, but its leaves remain fresh and bright green, even with intensive light. Stems become 40–50 cm long and 2–3 cm wide. The plant forms many side shoots willingly and obtains a beautiful, bushy and "hanging" growth.
